mechaber.he: דין מי שפרע מקצת חובו והשליש שטרו. ובו ב סעיפים: (לשון רמב"ם פי"א מה' מכירה) מי שפרע מקצת חובו והשליש את השטר וא"ל אם לא נתן לך עד יום פלוני תן לו שטרו והגיע הזמן ולא נתן לו לא יתן השליש את השטר שזו אסמכתא היא (פי' שתלה שעבודו בדעת עצמו ובמידי דבידו ולאו בידו וסמכא דעתיה שלא יחול השעבוד ולכן לא גמר ומקנה) ולא קניא ואם קנו מידו עליה בב"ד חשוב ה"ז קנה והוא שיתפיס זכיותיו בב"ד והוא שלא יהיה אנוס כיצד הרי שהתפיס שטרו או שוברו בב"ד וקנו מידו שאם לא יבא ביום פלוני ינתן זה לבעל דינו והגיע היום ולא בא הרי אלו נותנים ואם עכבו נהר או חולי מלבוא לא יתנו וכן כל כיוצא בזה והוא שיהיה בב"ד חשוב: הגה וי"א דלא בעינן שהתפיס שטרו מאחר דקנו מיניה בב"ד חשוב דהיינו ג' דבקיאי בדיני אסמכתא (טור בשם הרא"ש ומוהר"ם) וע' לקמן סי' ר"ז סט"ו שליש שהחזיר שטר למלוה שלא היה לו להחזיר משמתינן לשליש עד דמקבל עליו כל אונסא שאירע ללוה מזה (תשו' רשב"א אלף נ"ב) ואם נודע לב"ד שהחזיר שלא כדין אין דנין על השטר (ב"י בשם רשב"א) ואם לא נודע לב"ד והוציאו מן הלוה כל השטר ואח"כ נודע שהחזירו השליש שלא כדין השליש פטור דהוי גרמא בנזקין (תשו' רשב"א אלף נ"ב):
mechaber.en: One Who Paid Part of His Debt and Deposited His Document with a Third Party. Two seifim. If a person paid part of his debt, deposited the document with a third party, and said, 'If I do not pay you by a certain day, give him his document,' then when the day arrives without payment the custodian must not give it to the creditor, because this is an asmachta and does not effect acquisition. If a formal act of acquisition was made before an eminent beit din and he deposited his rights there without acting under duress, it is effective. Thus, if he deposited his document or receipt with the beit din and formally undertook that it be given to the opposing party if he failed to appear on a certain day, and he did not appear, it is delivered. If a river or illness prevented his arrival, it is not delivered. {Rama: Some say physical deposit of the document is unnecessary when the acquisition was made before an eminent beit din, meaning three judges expert in asmachta law. See below, siman 207, seif 15. If a custodian wrongly returns a document to the creditor, he is placed under a ban until he accepts liability for every loss this causes the borrower. If the beit din knows the return was improper, it does not adjudicate upon the document. If it did not know and collected the entire document before learning the truth, the custodian is exempt because his act only indirectly caused damage.}

baer_hetev.he:
קנה. עיין בטור שכתב בשם תשובת הראב"ד במי שלוה לחבירו ועשה לו שטר מכיר' על שדהו ומכר' לאחר קודם שבא הזמן כו' ע"ש ומביאו הרמ"א בס"ס רי"א. סמ"ע:
נהר. עי' בספרי ש"ך י"ד סי' רל"ב ס"ק כ' הוכחתי דדוקא אונס דשכיח ולא שכיח וכ"ש לא שכיח כלל הוי אונס לענין ממון אבל אי שכיח לא הוי אונס דה"ל לאתנויי וכתבתי שם בשם הרא"ש ורבינו ירוחם דעכבו נהר היינו שגדל הנהר ממי גשמים או הפשרת שלגים דאונסא דלא שכיח הוא אבל אי פסקיה מברא וכה"ג אונסא דשכיח הוא וה"ל לאסוקי אדעתי' ע"ש ועכשיו מצאתי בתשובת רש"ך ס"ב סי' מ"ה שכתב דברים הפוכי' ממה שכתבתי וחלק על הרא"ש ור"י. שוב מצאתי בתשובת מהר"א ן' ששון סימן ס"א שהאריך להשיג על מהרש"ך הנ"ל והסכים לדברי ונהניתי וע"ש ובתשובת מהר"ם אלשיך סימן ס'. עכ"ל:
דמקבל. דכל שעדיין לא גבה בו משמתינן עד שיסלקו דכל גרמא בנזקין מחוייב הגורם לסלקו אבל כשכבר גבה דפטור כדמסיים מור"ם וכ"כ בסי' קע"ה ס"מ בהג"ה ע"ש גם אם המלו' כאן ומוד' דשלא כדין בא לידו כייפינן ליה להחזיר השטר או לכתוב עליו שובר. עכ"ל הסמ"ע:
נודע. ע"ל סי' ס"ה סי"א וסט"ז וצ"ל דכאן הכל מודים דלא יגבה בו שודאי אינו חייב לו משא"כ התם נהי דאיתרע שטרא מ"מ יכול להיות שחייב לו ע"ש. ש"ך:
פטור. כתב בתשובת מ"ב סימן פ"ה דוקא כשהחזיר למלו' הוי גרמא אבל שטר שאינו פרוע שהחזירו ללוה מקרי גרמי וחייב השליש כדמוכח בתשו' הרא"ש ודמי לשורף שטרו של חבירו וע"ל סי' שפ"ו ס"ב. שם:
גרמא. כתב הסמ"ע ול"ד למ"ש הט"ו בסי' מ"ו סל"ז בהודאת עדים ששקר חתמו שצריכין לשלם גם בסי' כ"ט ס"ב ובסימן ל"ח כ"כ. צ"ל דיש לחלק בין דיני דגרמי לגרמא כמ"ש הט"ו בסי' שפ"ו וע"ש:
baer_hetev.en:
Acquired. See the Tur, who cites a responsum of the Raavad concerning one who lent money to another, received a sale deed to the borrower's field as security, and the borrower sold the field to someone else before the due date. See there. Rama cites this at the end of siman 211. Sema.
A river. See my Shach to Yoreh Deah, siman 232, seif katan 20, where I demonstrated that an event that is neither common nor extraordinarily rare, and certainly one that is wholly uncommon, is considered ones for monetary law. A common event is not ones, because the party should have stipulated for it. I cited the Rosh and Rabbeinu Yerucham that "the river prevented him" means that the river rose because of heavy rain or melting snow, an uncommon event. If the ferry service ceased or a similar predictable obstacle arose, that is a common event that he should have anticipated. I have now found Responsa Maharashach, part 2, siman 45, stating the opposite and disagreeing with the Rosh and Rabbeinu Yerucham. I later found Responsa Mahara ibn Sasson, siman 61, which discusses Maharashach at length, rejects his position, and agrees with my view. I was pleased to find this support. See there and Responsa Maharam Alshich, siman 60. Shach.
Who receives. So long as the creditor has not collected on the document, the third party is placed under nidui until he removes the harmful situation, because one who causes indirect damage must remove the cause. Once the creditor has already collected, however, the third party is exempt, as Rama concludes. The same rule appears in siman 175, seif 40, in the gloss. Likewise, if the lender is present and admits that the document came into his possession improperly, the court compels him to return the document or to write a receipt on it. Thus the Sema.
Became known. See below, siman 65, seifim 11 and 16. One must say that here everyone agrees the creditor may not collect because it is certain no debt is owed. There, although the document was impaired by suspicious circumstances, the underlying debt may nevertheless still be genuine. Shach.
Exempt. Responsa Maharam Brisk, siman 85, rules that the exemption applies specifically where the third party returned the document to the lender, which is only indirect causation. If an unpaid document was instead returned to the borrower, that is dina d'garmi and the third party is liable, as demonstrated by a responsum of the Rosh. It resembles burning another person's promissory note. See below, siman 386, seif 2. Shach.
Indirect causation. The Sema writes that this does not contradict the Tur and Mechaber in siman 46, seif 37, where witnesses who admit they signed falsely must pay, nor the similar laws in siman 29, seif 2, and siman 38. One must distinguish between actionable dina d'garmi and more remote grama, as the Tur and Mechaber explain in siman 386. See there.

Provided that he deposits it. Since the Gemara establishes this as the halachah in Nedarim, it follows that the ruling refers to this case.

chokhmat_shlomo.he: סעי' א') מי שפרע מקצת חובו והשליש את השטר וכו'. נ"ב הנה בדין אם השליש שטרו באופן שאין בו אסמכתא אם לא יפרע כו"כ לזמן פ' אזי יתחייב יותר ועבר הזמן ולא תבעו המלוה בזמנו אם נחשב זה ביטול התנאי ויתחייב בכולו נ"ל דלא הוי ביטול התנאי דהרי מפורש בסי' ע"ג ס"ו בסמ"ע והש"ך דאף בנשבע לפרוע ליום פ' אינו חייב לפרוע עד שיתבענו וא"כ אם בשבועה הוי כן מכש"כ בתנאי דהוי כן. ואף הטו"ז החולק שם היינו רק בשבועה דמכח איסור שבועה מחיוב לקיימו אפי' בלי תביעה ככל הנשבע לעשות איזה דבר אבל בלא חיוב שבועה מודה הט"ז דאינו חייב לקיים רק כשיתבענו. וכן מצאתי בב"ש ה' גיטין סי' קמ"ג ס"ק י"ד דאין נחשב ביטול התנאי רק כשתובעו (וע' בתשובתי לחו"מ מהדורא ג' ראיה לזה בסי' רמ"ג ע"ש). וגם בשבועה נראה עיקר כהש"ך והסמ"ע ומה שהביא הט"ז בסי' עג וביו"ד סי' לח ראי' דבעינן שיהי' כתוב בשטר כשיתבענו נראה דאינו ראיה דהתם מיירי לענין אם מחויב לפרוע לשני ולא לראשון בזה בעינן שיהי' כתוב בשטר כשיתבענו דאז כל שלא תבעו אף אם יפרע לראשון אין כאן קיום שבועה כלל ולכך אף אם ישלם לראשון לא קיים השבועה כלל וביטל השבועה שנשבע לשני ולכך חייב לקיים שבועתו וליתן לשני אבל אם לא כתב כשיתבענו נהי דלהיות מחויב לשלם לו בלא תביעה אינו מחויב מ"מ אם פרעו לו מעצמו קיים בזה מצות שבועה דהרי נשבע שיפרע לו והרי פרע לו וכיון שכן אינו מחויב ליתן לשני דאם יתן לראשון נמי קיים השבועה ומאי אולמא דהך מהך סוף סוף קיים השבוע' לכך ל"ש לומר שמחויב ליתן לשני דבידו ליתן לראשון וקיים השבועה ג"כ ומה לי זה או זה ובפרט דסתם נדרים להחמיר ופירושיהן להקל א"כ בנשבע סתם לכופו ליתן בלי תביעה אין בידינו לכופו דיכול לומר שהי' כוונתו רק כשיתבענו ואינו נדון כעובר על השבוע' אבל התם אם נשבע סתם יכול ליתן לראשון דיכול לומר כוונתו הי' לשלם לו אפי' בלי תביעה או סתם נמי הוי להחמיר ולכך אין בידינו לכופו ליתן לשני רק אם פירש לראשון כשיתבענו. ועוד והוא העיקר בעיני דהנה מה דאינו חייב לשלם רק כשיתבענו היינו כיון דבלי שבועה לא הי' חייב לפרוע חובו רק אם יתבענו א"כ ה"נ אף אם נשבע אנן סהדי דלא הוה כמותו רק על מה שהוא חייב מן הדין ולא מה שהוא יותר מן הדין כמ"ש בחו"מ סי' ע"ג בנשבע' לשלם ומגיע השמטה פטור מלשלם דלא נתחייב לשלם רק מה שיהיו חייבין מן הדין א"כ ה"נ כיון דבלא שבועה אינו חייב רק אם תבעו אף כשנשבע הוי רק ע"ד כן וא"כ תינח התם אבל ביו"ד סי' רל"ח מיירי שהי' חייב לב' בני אדם ולא הי"ל לשלם רק לא' כמ"ש הש"ך ביו"ד סי' רל"ח ס"ק ק"ג דביש לו לשלם לשניה' מהו נ"מ ופשיטא שחייב לשלם לב' ובע"כ דמיירי שאין לו לשלם רק לא' וא"כ י"ל דהמעשה הי' דגם בשעת השבועה לא הי"ל לשלם רק לא' וא"כ מן הדין לא הי' חייב ליתן הכל לא' רק יחלוקו כמ"ש בה' גביות חוב וא"כ השתא דנשבע לשלם הכל לראשון הוי נשבע יותר על החיוב כיון דחזינן דנשבע יותר על החיוב שוב ממילא הוה דעתו ג"כ בלי תביעה כיון דחזינן שבא לחייב נפשו יותר ממה שהוא חייב לכך חייב לשלם אף בלי תביעה לכך בעינן שכתב בפירוש כשיתבענו אז חל שבועת הב' אבל בלא"ה לא חל שבוע' הב' רק אמרי' כאן נמצא כאן הי' כיון דעתה אין לו רק כדי חוב א' מהסתם וגם בשעת השבועה הוי כן כמ"ש כן בסי' ס' ובסי' קי"ב דעות דאמרי' כאן נמצא וכאן הי' וא"כ ה"נ אמרי' מדהשתא אין לו יותר גם בשבועת הראשון לא הי"ל יותר לכך לא חל שבועת הב' רק אם מפורש בראשון כשיתבענו וזה סברא ברורה בעז"ה. ולכך גם בשבועה העיקר כהסמ"ע והש"ך ובלי שבוע' י"ל כ"ע מודים כי למעט בפלוגתא עדיף כנלפע"ד בזה ביטל התנאי בפרט דקשה להוציא ממון: (באותו סעי') והוא שלא יהי' אנוס. נ"ב ע' בש"ך ונראה דאם הי' צריך לפייס אחרים התחייב באיז' דבר לעשותו והוא תלוי בדעת אחרים אך סבר שיפייסם ולא יכול לפייסם הוי אונס ואף שהי' אפשר לפייסם בממון רב וכדמוכח בש"ס פ"ג דגיטין ר"ל א"ד א"ר יוסף אטו תרקבי דדינרי בעי למיסב לה הא כמ"ד יש אונס בגיטין הא כמ"ד אין אונס בגיטין וכו'. מוכח דעכ"פ אונס הוי א"כ היכי דמועיל אונס אף זה הוי אונס וז"ב וכן מבואר באהע"ז סי' נ' כב"ש סקט"ז ע"ש כן: שם סעי' א' בהג"ה השליש פטור דהוי גרמא בניזקין. נ"ב עמ"ש בזה בחיבורי על חו"מ מהדורא ה' סי' תקס"ט בתשו' לק' קאלק אימתי חייב לשלם ואימתי פטור ודו"ק:
chokhmat_shlomo.en: Seif 1. One who paid part of his debt and deposited the document with a third party, etc. I was asked about a case in which the document was deposited under a valid arrangement that does not constitute asmachta: if the debtor does not pay a specified amount by a fixed date, he will become obligated in a larger sum. The date passed, but the lender did not demand payment on that day. Does the failure to demand payment count as cancellation of the condition, so that the debtor does not become liable for the larger amount? In my opinion it does not cancel the condition. In siman 73, seif 6, the Sema and Shach explain that even one who swore to pay on a given day is not obligated to pay until the creditor demands payment. If that is true of an oath, it is certainly true of an ordinary condition. The Taz, who disagrees there, does so only because an oath creates an independent prohibition requiring the person to fulfill what he swore even without a demand, like any oath to perform an act. Without an oath, even the Taz agrees that payment need not be made until demanded. I found the same principle in Beit Shmuel, Even HaEzer 143, seif katan 14, that a condition is not treated as violated until demand is made. I also brought a proof in my responsa to Choshen Mishpat, third edition, siman 243. Even with respect to an oath, the primary ruling appears to follow the Sema and Shach. The Taz’s proof from the requirement that a document say “when he demands payment” is not decisive. There the issue is whether the debtor must pay the second claimant rather than the first. If the first oath expressly said “when he demands payment,” then while the first creditor has not demanded, paying him would not fulfill that oath, so the second oath may obligate payment to the second creditor. But if the first oath did not contain that phrase, although the debtor cannot be compelled to pay without demand, if he nevertheless pays voluntarily he has fulfilled his oath. Consequently one cannot compel him to pay the second creditor, because he can still pay the first and fulfill the oath. There is no basis to prefer one oath over the other. Moreover, ordinary vows are interpreted stringently as to their obligation but leniently as to ambiguous wording. If a person swore simply to pay, we cannot compel him without demand, for he may say he intended payment when demanded. Nevertheless, if he voluntarily pays, he has surely fulfilled the oath. There is therefore no contradiction. The principal point is that one who swears to pay generally undertakes no more than the obligation imposed by law. Just as one who swore to pay a debt is exempt if shemittah intervenes, because he did not undertake payment beyond his legal liability, so too one who ordinarily need not pay before demand is understood to have sworn only on that basis. The case in Yoreh Deah 238 is different because there he owed two creditors and apparently possessed funds sufficient for only one. Ordinarily the law would not require paying the full amount to either one, but division. By swearing to pay the first creditor in full, he demonstrated an intention to assume an obligation greater than the ordinary legal duty. Once we see that he intended to bind himself beyond the law, it is reasonable to understand that he also intended to pay without demand, unless he expressly limited his oath to payment upon demand. This distinction resolves the sources. Accordingly, even regarding an oath the ruling follows the Sema and Shach, and without an oath all authorities can be understood to agree. Certainly in monetary law, where there is doubt, we should not extract money on the basis of a disputed extension of the condition. In the same seif: provided that he was not prevented by circumstances beyond his control. If the obligor needed to obtain the cooperation of others in order to perform what he undertook, and he reasonably assumed he could persuade them but in fact could not, this is considered ones. That remains true even where, in theory, he could have persuaded them only by paying an extraordinarily large sum. The Gemara in Gittin indicates that having to give enormous sums is itself a form of compulsion. Therefore, wherever ones is legally effective, this too is ones. The same appears in Even HaEzer 50 in Beit Shmuel. There, seif 1, in the gloss: the third party is exempt because this is indirect damage. See what I wrote on Choshen Mishpat, fifth edition, siman 569, in a responsum to the community of Kalik, where I explained when the third party must pay and when he is exempt.

haggahot_imrei_barukh.en: (Rama, seif 1) The third party custodian is exempt, etc. Note: In Responsa Rashba there is a case in which part of a debt was paid, the document was deposited with a third party, and the custodian returned the document to the lender. See there. One can say that specifically in such a case the custodian is exempt, because when he returned it to the lender he did not intend that the lender should claim and collect more than was actually owed under the document. If so, this does not conflict with the law of witnesses who signed falsely.

The shalish is exempt. Responsa Masat Binyamin rules that this applies specifically where the shalish returned the document to the creditor. If he wrongfully returns an unpaid document to the borrower, he is like one who burns a debt instrument and is liable. The Shach cites this. Rama in siman 386 says that a scribe who mistakenly writes one hundred instead of two hundred is exempt and is not comparable to one who burns a document. The distinction is that one who burns an existing document destroys a right already possessed by the creditor and is therefore a direct causative tortfeasor. A scribe who errs never created the additional right in the first place. He merely failed to provide the creditor with the evidence that might have been created, which resembles one who refuses to help another recover a lost object or refuses to testify. Ramban writes that one who sees another intending to give a gift and prevents the gift is not liable, because he did not damage existing property but merely prevented a benefit from arising. The same applies to a scribe who writes one hundred instead of two hundred. A shalish who simply returns the document to the creditor likewise does not himself create the damage; the creditor's later use of the instrument creates it, much as one who hires false witnesses is exempt in human court. But if the shalish himself gives false testimony concerning the terms of the deposit and later admits he lied, he is like witnesses who testified falsely and is liable under the laws of direct causation. Even if his false testimony favored the creditor rather than the borrower, once he himself supplied the operative false evidence and thereby caused the loss, he must pay. The Tumim struggles with these comparisons, but the distinction between destroying an existing right, directly providing false operative evidence, and merely enabling another person's later wrongful act resolves the matter.

The third-party custodian is exempt. This is only indirect causation, not actionable causative damage. It differs from the laws above in siman 46:37, where witnesses who admit falsely signing must pay under dina degarmi, and similarly in simanim 29 and 38. Tosafot and Rosh distinguish between actionable causative damage and mere indirect causation, depending on whether the loss occurs immediately and is certain. The Tur and Mechaber explain this below in siman 386. According to what I wrote in Derishah and Sema there, Rashba and those with him distinguish between loss occurring before the person undertook to pay and loss occurring after he accepted liability under excommunication. On that basis one might have said that above in siman 46 the Mechaber copied the Rosh, while here Rama copied Rashba. But if so Rama should have stated that the matter is disputed. Therefore the first explanation is primary, and the Rosh too agrees here.

Provided he was not compelled. Ketzot HaChoshen cites the dispute in Yoreh Deah 232 whether one who was prevented only on the final day of a period is considered compelled, and the view of the Agudah that this is not called compulsion. He sought proof from the law of houses in a walled city. In my view that proof does not stand. A house in a walled city is treated in Arakhin as a loan-like transaction, even though Rashba calls it a sale on condition. The correct structure is that if redemption money is given within the year, the sale is undone retroactively and the buyer's use is retrospectively treated like a loan, which is why the Gemara discusses interest. In an ordinary sale or gift conditioned on the transferor's own act, if he is prevented by an unforeseen compulsion from fulfilling the condition, the transfer can fail through the principle that the Torah exempts unavoidable circumstances. This differs from a condition imposed on the recipient, where his failure merely prevents him from acquiring. Nevertheless, the Agudah did not need the walled-city case to establish that final-day compulsion is sometimes insufficient, for Scripture itself requires that the seller actually acquire the means to redeem. If he has no money throughout the period, that is a strong form of inability and yet redemption expires. Still, I do not think the Agudah's rule should be extended from vows to monetary conditions, gittin, or kiddushin. In those fields, if a truly unusual and unforeseeable compulsion arose only on the last day, there is strong basis to say the party never intended the condition to fail through such a circumstance. In vows, by contrast, the Torah expressly released compelled vows. The Agudah can therefore hold that this special release applies only where the person was genuinely unable to perform at all. If he negligently delayed until the last day and only then became unable, he may still need formal release from the vow because the vow itself was not automatically annulled. Thus the Agudah's distinction belongs specifically to vows, which is why Shulchan Aruch brings it there and not in monetary law or gittin. In civil and marital conditions, a final-day unavoidable event can still negate the condition where the circumstances clearly show it was not contemplated.

pitchei_teshuva.en: The third-party custodian is exempt. See Baer Heitev in the name of Masat Binyamin, who distinguishes that when the custodian merely returned the document to the creditor the resulting loss is indirect, as appears from a responsum of the Rosh. Chatam Sofer, Choshen Mishpat, siman 140, strongly questions this. If, according to the Rashba, a custodian who returns a document to the creditor causes only indirect damage and is exempt, how can the Gemara in Ketubot 85a, in the case of Avimi, hold an agent liable because 'I sent you to improve matters, not to impair them,' since he should have taken the document before paying? Had he taken the document and then returned it to the creditor, he would supposedly be exempt, yet because he never took it at all he is liable. Chatam Sofer therefore concludes that the laws distinguishing direct from indirect damage apply to an ordinary outsider who damages another, but one who received property as a custodian or agent is liable even for remote consequences of negligent custody or deviation from his agency. Many instances of custodian negligence and misperformance of agency are, upon analysis, only indirect causation, yet the custodian or agent is liable. Thus the Rosh correctly held a third-party custodian liable for returning Shimon's sale document to Shimon's father. Although documents are excluded from ordinary custodian liability, that exemption concerns a document lost through negligence; here he effectively destroyed the legal protection by his own act. The Rashba's case cited by the Rama at the beginning of siman 55 is different. There both borrower and creditor instructed the custodian that if payment were not made by a certain date he should return the document to the creditor. The law nevertheless forbade him to do so because the condition was an asmachta. If he violated the law and returned it, he is exempt because he did not violate the principals' instruction. His fault is therefore only that of an ordinary tortfeasor causing indirect loss. Based on this, Chatam Sofer ruled in a case where Reuven gave his agent a non-Jewish debt claim to collect and expressly warned him that if he could not collect it he was not to transfer it to Reuven's partner Shimon. The agent disobeyed, delivered it to Shimon, Shimon collected the entire debt, and then withheld Reuven's half because of a separate claim. Since the agent violated the principal's instruction, he must compensate Reuven for the loss. Once the agent is liable, Shimon cannot seize Reuven's money in a manner that shifts the loss to the agent; Reuven need only take a hesset oath regarding Shimon's claim. Chatam Sofer concludes that this is the true law. Pitchei Teshuva notes, however, that Netivot HaMishpat below, siman 58, seif katan 2, had already addressed the difficulty from Ketubot and answered well that there the agent changed the manner of payment against the sender's instruction, which constitutes negligence causing monetary loss and therefore creates liability. Also, the Rama's broad wording below in siman 386, seif 3, concerning a third-party custodian who returned a document, implies exemption in all cases. See the Shach there. The matter requires study.
